summary.text: A 3-year-old male Persian cat was referred for a dark plaque on the right cornea after 2 months of blepharospasm, epiphora and mild conjunctival hyperemia. Examination found a corneal lesion consistent with corneal sequestrum, mild medial canthal entropion and a roughly 3 mm black plaque on the upper palpebral conjunctiva; the anterior and posterior segments showed no other lesions.

Surgical removal was recommended and lubricating drops were used until surgery 2 weeks after the initial consultation. Under general anesthesia the corneal sequestrum was removed by superficial lamellar keratectomy and the conjunctival plaque by excisional biopsy, with medial canthoplasty and modified Hotz-Celsus procedure for the entropion and no graft because the lesions were shallow. Tobramycin and lubricating drops followed.

Histopathology of both samples showed collagen compaction with brownish discoloration, ulceration and inflammatory infiltrate, and confirmed a conjunctival sequestrum. At 7 days both surgical sites were healing as expected. At 12 weeks there was no ocular pain or recurrence of sequestrum formation, and corneal transparency had markedly improved.

summary.text: An 8-year-old female spayed domestic shorthair cat, originally evaluated at a private veterinary ophthalmology clinic, presented with a corneal sequestrum, keratitis and lower lid entropion, together with a pigmented lesion on the lower palpebral conjunctiva. Table 1 also records a vascularized corneal lesion.

The lower eyelid conjunctival lesion was removed by excisional biopsy. Histology showed focal conjunctival epithelial ulceration with compaction and brunescence of the underlying proprial collagen and a few inflammatory cells in the surrounding substantia propria. No recurrence was reported for the conjunctival sequestrum cases in the series.

summary.text: A 6-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat, originally evaluated at a university comparative ophthalmology service, was presented for evaluation of a left corneal sequestrum presumed secondary to chronic bilateral entropion that led to non-ulcerative keratitis in both eyes. Both eyes had macroblepharon, and the entropion was presumed secondary to acromegaly. Two pigmented foci with surrounding hyperemia were noted on the right third eyelid conjunctiva.

Entropion was corrected by medial canthoplasty with a modified Hotz-Celsus procedure following lamellar keratectomy and excisional biopsy of the pigmented conjunctival lesions. Histology of the third eyelid lesion showed focal compaction and brunescence of proprial collagen with intact epithelium in the examined sections and hypercellular, vascularized granulation tissue around it. No recurrence was reported for the conjunctival sequestrum cases in the series.

A dorsotemporal paraxial corneal sequestrum in the same eye had previously resolved spontaneously with medical treatment 16 months earlier. No recurrence was reported for the conjunctival sequestrum cases in the series.

summary.text: A 10-year-old spayed female domestic medium-haired cat, evaluated at a university, had a history of presumed chronic herpesvirus. Plaques were present on the anterior surface of both third eyelids with mild conjunctival hyperemia; the text calls them brown and Table 1 calls them black. There were no other corneal, eyelid or conjunctival abnormalities, no keratitis and no evidence of previous corneal sequestra.

The leading edge of the right third eyelid was surgically excised. Histology showed conjunctival ulceration over mineralized substantia propria with an adherent layer of brown material and mild lymphoplasmacytic and neutrophilic conjunctivitis. No recurrence was reported for the conjunctival sequestrum cases in the series.

caption_evidence.quote:
FIGURE 2
(A) Histologic section of the corneal plaque removed by superficial lamellar keratectomy in Patient 1. There is brownish discoloration and compaction of the collagen lamellae and lack of viable keratocytes in the affected area (arrow). Inflammatory cells infiltrate the surrounding stroma (asterisk). The surface (top of the image) lacks epithelium (ulceration). Hematoxylin and eosin stained. Scale bar 100 μm. (B, C) Histologic section of the dark conjunctival lesion removed by excisional biopsy in Patient 1. (B) The overlying conjunctival epithelium is discontinuous (ulceration) (black arrow) and separated from the sequestrum (indicated by white asterisk). Hematoxylin and eosin stained. Scale bar 100 μm. (C) There is brownish discoloration and compaction of the collagen and lack of viable fibroblasts in the sequestrum and an abrupt transition between affected and unaffected tissue. A small number of inflammatory cells and nuclear debris occupy the surrounding substantia propria. Hematoxylin and eosin stained. Scale bar 20 μm.

article_limitations: No supplements; Table 1 present in source.json and every row used. Six figures inspected in the visual submission; the annotation figure rows keep the caption-layer not_inspected convention.
All patients are cats (nonhuman). Breed is carried in case_context descriptions because the demographics schema has no breed attribute.

Source conflicts quarantined as review-only facts: Patient 2 conjunctival lesion eye (text left, Table 1 right); Patient 4 conjunctival site (lower palpebral versus third eyelid) and corneal laterality (same eye versus contralateral), both from the discussion; Patient 5 plaque color (brown in text, black in Table 1).

Series statements not copied to individuals because the covered set is unclear or counts only: "In all cases, an amorphous black plaque" (four additional cases or all five), three of four cases with ipsilateral corneal sequestra (Table 1 lists Patient 3 as contralateral), three cases with ulceration, entropion in three of four cases, and inflammatory cells and microorganisms in the surrounding propria.

Statements covering all five patients explicitly were copied to each: histology of all five conjunctival lesions, unknown infectious disease status, no recurrence in any case, and no known history of listed causes of conjunctival necrosis (kept review-only because detailed history was missing for some cases).
Surgical instruments, brand names, specimen fixation, and the corneal sequestrum histology availability counts are not recorded as separate facts.
Table 1 footnote a (archive source anonymized) is administrative and not recorded.

Series counts that disagree with the individual descriptions were not copied: "Three of the cases had conjunctival ulceration" while the case texts and captions report ulceration for Patients 1, 2, 4 and 5 and intact epithelium for Patient 3; "Three of the four cases also had corneal sequestra ipsilaterally" while Table 1 lists ipsilateral for Patients 2 and 4, contralateral for Patient 3 and absent for Patient 5.
No literal order links presentation and excision/histology for Patients 2, 4 and 5 (paragraph order only), so those events carry no relations.
